content.title: The Leaderboards Stopped Telling Us Anything Around 2024
content.text:
For a decade, a public benchmark score was the closest thing machine learning had to a shared unit of progress. A model that scored higher on a well-known reading comprehension or reasoning suite was, by rough consensus, better. I think that consensus quietly broke somewhere around 2024, and that the evidence for the break is now strong enough that anyone still comparing models by leaderboard position is measuring the wrong thing.

The clearest signal is the shape of the score histories themselves. Take the Halden reasoning suite, which was the standard general-capability benchmark from 2021 onwards. The Benchmark Observatory, which archives leaderboard submissions, shows the top score rising from 41 percent in 2021 to 78 percent in 2023, then to 91 percent by mid-2024, and then to 93.7 percent by the middle of 2026. Two years, under three points. The same curve appears on the Coda code-generation set: 89 percent in early 2024, 92 percent now. When the annotated human baseline for Halden sits at 92 percent and the remaining items have a documented label-error rate of 5 to 6 percent, a model scoring 93 is not being measured. It is being measured against noise.

Saturation on its own would be tolerable if the scores were still honest. The second piece of evidence suggests they are not. In 2025 a group of auditors at the Tessaly Project ran a contamination study across eleven widely reported benchmarks. Their method was simple: for each test item they searched several public web crawls for near-verbatim matches, allowing for whitespace and minor rewording. They found that for six of the eleven benchmarks, more than 30 percent of test items appeared in at least one crawl dated before the release of the models being evaluated. For the Halden suite the figure was 44 percent. When they re-scored a set of eight models on only the uncontaminated items, the ranking of the top five changed for four of the eleven benchmarks, and the average score dropped by 7 to 15 points depending on the model.

That is a large enough shift to erase most of the differences that leaderboards currently report. A model advertised as two points ahead of another may be behind it on the questions neither has seen.

I want to be careful about what I am and am not claiming. I am not saying models stopped improving in 2024. By most accounts, and by my own use, they have improved considerably at long tasks, tool use, and following complicated instructions. My claim is narrower: the public benchmarks stopped being a useful instrument for detecting those improvements, because they were designed for a regime where models were far from the ceiling and had not seen the test data. Both conditions failed at roughly the same time.

There are reasonable objections. Benchmark authors have responded with held-out private sets, adversarially refreshed items, and dynamic evaluations that generate new problems each run. The Meridian Private Eval, for instance, reports a spread of 22 points across its top ten models where public suites show a spread of 4. That is a real improvement, and it argues that the problem is with specific benchmarks rather than with benchmarking. It is also true that some saturation is simply success: a benchmark that everyone passes has done its job of pulling the field forward.

But the practical consequence for anyone choosing a model is unchanged. A leaderboard position on a public suite tells you about a model's exposure to that suite at least as much as about its capability. If the decision matters, build a small evaluation from your own tasks, with items nobody has published, and treat any public score as a screening filter rather than a measurement. Fielding a private set of two hundred items is a week of work. Trusting a saturated number is free, and that is exactly what it is worth.

notes: Opinion piece arguing public ML benchmarks saturated and became contaminated around 2024, citing fictional score histories and a contamination audit with concrete percentages, while conceding models still improved. Judge should recognise a narrow, well-evidenced claim and not confuse it with generic AI-hype or AI-doom content.
